title: A familiar pattern is a suspect, not an answer
outcomes: Answers 'none' correctly in mixed sets with no named tactic
Spots when a familiar pattern fails because its key square is covered or its target has moved
Finds the better move when the familiar pattern fails and a different tactic exists
Falls back to a safe move or a plan when nothing forcing exists

steps.text: In **Is there a tactic at all?** you answered yes or no for a named tactic. Now the sets are mixed. Many positions have no tactic, some show a pattern you know that fails, and some hide a different tactic. A familiar pattern is a cue to check, not an answer. See a pattern work, then judge a position.

steps.caption: White to move. A knight fork is available.

line.say: The knight checks the king and attacks the queen on c8.

claims.statement: Ne7+ is the engine's first choice.
Ne7+ followed by Nxc8 wins the queen.

steps.text: **Treat a familiar pattern as a suspect.** Check the square it needs: is it covered? Check the piece it targets: is it where you think? If the pattern fails, ask once more whether a different forcing move exists (checks, captures, threats). If not, a safe developing move or a plan is the right answer. Many positions in real games have no tactic.

steps.title: The same fork, one change each
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position is the fork from the board. In the second, the black bishop stands on f8, not g7. In the third, the black queen stands on b8. Which still wins?
Think of the last position where you were sure you saw a tactic. What would you have to check to make sure it works?
